Name: Deng, Lu & Chen 2016, Continuous Monitoring of A/B Tests without Pain: Optional Stopping in Bayesian Testing
Summary: Formal argument plus simulations that Bayesian hypothesis testing stays valid under continuous monitoring when the stopping rule is proper, with a catalogue of improper rules practitioners use, a comparison to the NHST corrections for peeking, and guidelines. Theory and simulation only: the abstract reports no field experiments, no N and no window; the arXiv page lists one version (2016-02-17) and names no venue. Its boundary is the prior: the paper makes early stopping legal under an honest prior, it does not make a small sample informative.
Scrub: no measurement (theory/position)
Grounds: Whether wrasse may read a running prediction's metric before its window closes (charter section 6, step 3): only if the stopping rule was written into the banked prediction, never decided at the time of looking.

Name: Gelman, Hill & Yajima 2012, Why We (Usually) Don't Have to Worry About Multiple Comparisons
ID: arXiv:0907.2478 (opened as v1, 2009-07-13); published J. Research on Educational Effectiveness 5(2), DOI 10.1080/19345747.2011.618213 per recall, publisher page refused
Summary: Argues that multilevel (hierarchical Bayesian) models replace multiple-comparison corrections by partial pooling: estimates shrink toward each other and "intervals for comparisons are more likely to include zero", most strongly where group-level variation is low. Frames small-sample inference in Type S (sign) and Type M (magnitude) terms and states that "type M errors are more likely when uncertainty is high"; a worked educational example with 2,000 people is called "woefully underpowered". Method paper with reanalyses of education data; no web experiments, no bot handling.
Scrub: no measurement (theory/position)
Grounds: If wrasse ever compares more than one page, copy variant or sleeve at once, the comparison is pooled rather than corrected, and any winner at the site's N is presumed a Type M overestimate until re-measured (charter section 6, step 4).

Name: Szabo 1999, Micropayments and Mental Transaction Costs
ID: mirror; original at szabo.best.vwh.net (dead); dated May 1999
Summary: The binding cost of a small purchase is the customer's cost of deciding: "Customer mental transaction costs come from at least three sources" (uncertain cash flows, costly attribute observation, costly decision making), and these "will soon dominate the technological transaction costs of the payment system", so cutting per-transaction compute "may often be economically insignificant". Illustrations rather than measurements: AT&T's $0.15 flat versus Sprint's $0.10 variable rate in 1999 ads; "up to 50% of the costs of a long distance call are for billing" by unspecified estimates. Grounds: Bears on any wrasse recommendation about coin granularity or per-view pricing (guideline 3): each decision point costs the buyer more than a coin is worth, so proposals remove decisions rather than add price points.

Summary: Double-entry mental accounting: "the pain of paying" offsets consumption pleasure; consumption already paid for "can be enjoyed as if it were free"; coupling is "the degree to which consumption calls to mind thoughts of payment"; the model predicts a preference to prepay and for flat rates "even if it involves paying more for the same usage." Name: Patrick & Park 2006, Paying before consuming: Examining the robustness of consumers' preference for prepayment
Summary: Four lab studies with undergraduates (N = 64-65, 65, 215, 148 analysed) on $1,200 installment scenarios. Only hedonic-nondurable products elicit a prepayment preference: "88.23% of vacation participants chose prepayment, versus 26.66% (washer dryer)". The preference holds when the deal looks favourable (26 prepay vs 14 postpay at high transaction utility) and is not significant when it does not (21 vs 19); and "when the choice of payment timing is not offered, consumers become indifferent" (vacation purchase intent 4.74 prepay vs 4.44 postpay, n.s.). Authors' limits: homogeneous student samples; installment payments only, not lump sums.
Scrub: lab sample (surveys, hypothetical)
Grounds: Narrows what the coin sleeve can be credited with: prepayment is liked for a hedonic nondurable like a video vend only when the deal looks favourable and the buyer chose the timing, so "prepaid" is not itself a conversion lever wrasse may bank a prediction on.

Name: Luguri & Strahilevitz 2021, Shining a Light on Dark Patterns
Summary: Two census-weighted online experiments on American adults recruited by Dynata, testing whether dark patterns raise acceptance of a dubious identity-theft protection service. Name: Tome (Cloudflare) 2025, The crawl-to-click gap: Cloudflare data on AI bots, training, and referrals (method in Belson & Rhea, AI search crawl-refer ratio on Radar, 2025-07-01)
Summary: Across Cloudflare's network, January-July 2025, monthly crawl-to-refer ratios, defined as HTML requests from a platform's crawler user agents divided by HTML requests whose Referer names that platform: Anthropic 286,930 in January and, "Even after an 87% decline this year, it still crawled 38,000 pages for every referred page visit in July 2025"; OpenAI "from 1,217 bots per human in January to 1,091 in July"; Perplexity "from 54 bots per human in January to 195"; Microsoft 38.5 to 40.7; Google 3.8 to 5.4 (table). Purpose split on the same network: "Over the past 12 months, 80% of AI crawling was for training, compared with 18% for search and just 2% for user actions." Caveats from the method post: native apps send no Referer so ratios "may overstate"; Google's own AS referral traffic excluded; training, search and user-fetch crawler UAs are pooled per platform.
Scrub: one network only, request share not visitor share, bot is not agent, native-app referrals invisible (Cloudflare's own caveat)
Grounds: Sets wrasse's expectation of what AI-crawler volume on squaloo.com will ever return as human visits: at these ratios, close to none, so crawler hits in garage_hits are never read as demand and never fed into a conversion denominator.

Name: Google Search Central 2025, AI features and your website (last updated 2025-12-10)
Summary: Shipped guidance: the only eligibility condition for AI Overviews and AI Mode is that a page be indexed and snippet-eligible; "There are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary"; "There's also no special schema.org structured data that you need to add." Recommends structured data that matches visible text, crawling allowed in robots.txt and by any CDN, nosnippet/max-snippet/noindex to limit, and Google-Extended to limit training elsewhere. "Indexing and serving isn't guaranteed." Chosen over OpenAI's product-feed spec (opened; registered feeds, "currently targets the US", search on by default and checkout off) because it tells a tiny site what to publish with no gate.
Scrub: promotional, guarantee disclaimed (appearance not assured even when all conditions are met)
Grounds: What wrasse ships for discovery under guideline 5: an indexable, snippet-eligible coin page with honest structured data and a crawler-permissive robots.txt, rather than any AI-specific file; and no prediction may promise appearance.

Name: Holscher (Read the Docs) 2024, AI crawlers need to be more respectful
Summary: First-party write-up from one documentation host, from its own CDN and bandwidth charts, May-June 2024: "One crawler downloaded 73 TB of zipped HTML files in May 2024, with almost 10 TB in a single day", costing over $5,000 in bandwidth; a second episode of about 10 TB in June from a suspected social-network downloader (attribution uncertain per the author). After blocking, "bandwidth for our downloaded files has decreased by 75% (~800GB/day to ~200GB/day)". All figures are bytes from one host's dashboards; no request counts and no crawler-versus-human share; the per-day cost is the author's estimate.
Scrub: one network only, no method stated, bytes not requests (volume says nothing about visitors), single-actor dominated (one crawler is most of the figure)
Grounds: Tells wrasse that a bandwidth or request spike can be one crawler re-fetching static files and is no evidence of demand; it justifies rate-limit and robots proposals without feeding the spike into any funnel metric.

Name: Richter & Berger 2019, Scanning the Scanners: Sensing the Internet from a Massively Distributed Network Telescope
ID: DOI 10.1145/3355369.3355595 (ACM IMC 2019); Akamai-hosted PDF opened, ACM page refused
Summary: Unsolicited packets logged at 89,000 Akamai CDN servers (178,000 public IPv4 addresses in 2,800 prefixes, 1,347 ASes, 156 countries) during November 2018, with a baseline from early 2016 to December 2018. "We find that some 87% of logged traffic is the result of scanning activity"; "In total, we identified 2.2M scans". For a host anywhere: "Routed IPv4 addresses receive a baseline of some 3000 packets on a daily basis as a result of Internet-wide scans of the IPv4 space", and "a 3-fold increase in baseline activity, starting from ~1000 packets in early 2016". Packet-level, all ports, not HTTP requests; it does not measure time-to-first-probe for a newly exposed host.
Scrub: one network only, packet-level not HTTP (not a share of an access log), stale window (Nov 2018; the paper's own trend says the baseline has risen since)
Grounds: Backs the register's needs-review row on squaloo.com's audience from the probe side: scanner traffic is location-independent background present at any routed address, carries no information about demand, and is partitioned out (the instrument's probe kind) before any interest metric is computed.

Name: AlNoamany, Weigle & Nelson 2013, Access Patterns for Robots and Humans in Web Archives
ID: arXiv:1309.4009 (2013-09-16); JCDL 2013 per recall, venue not stated on page
Summary: Internet Archive Wayback Machine access logs: cluster sample of one week (2012-02-02 to 02-08), one 2M-request slice per day; the analysed slice is 2012-02-02, about 33 minutes and 37,634 sessions. Robots separated from humans by user-agent checks plus traffic-pattern rules ("Users with more than 20 different User-Agents were classified as robots"; a session "with less than one image file for every 10 HTML files" is a robot; a browsing-speed threshold). Result: "Robots outnumber humans 10:1 in terms of sessions, 5:4 in terms of raw HTTP accesses, and 4:1 in terms of megabytes transferred"; robots almost always fetch TimeMaps (95% of their accesses) while humans fetch archived pages (82%). One archive, one slice, 2012.
Scrub: one network only, stale window (2012), heuristic bot labels (rule-based, no ground truth)
Grounds: The cleanest measured warning behind the register's qualifier that request share is not visitor share: on one archive the robot share was 10:1 by session and only 5:4 by request, so wrasse's instrument reports sessions, requests and bytes separately and never lets one stand in for another.
